question.stem: Two loudspeakers, S1 and S2, stand at one end of a school hall. They are connected to the same signal generator, which drives them in phase at a frequency of 425 Hz. A student walks slowly along a line parallel to the line joining the loudspeakers and notices that the sound is loud at some positions and very quiet at others. The point P on this line is 7.40 m from S1 and 5.40 m from S2. The speed of sound in the hall is 340 $\text{m s}^{-1}$.
question.diagramAlt: Plan view: a signal generator connected by wires to two loudspeakers S1 and S2, one above the other at the left. A dashed vertical line to their right is labelled as the line along which the student walks. A point P on this line is joined to S1 by a line labelled 7.40 m and to S2 by a line labelled 5.40 m.

parts.label: a
parts.question: State the condition for the two loudspeakers to act as coherent sources.
markscheme: the waves they emit have a constant phase difference / the same frequency and a constant phase relationship ✓

parts.label: b
parts.question: Calculate the wavelength of the sound in the hall.

mistakes.feedback: Wavelength = speed ÷ frequency, not frequency ÷ speed.

parts.label: c
parts.question: Determine whether P is a loud position or a quiet position.
markscheme: this is $2.5\lambda$ / an odd number of half wavelengths / $(n + \tfrac{1}{2})\lambda$ with $n = 2$ ✓
so the waves from the two loudspeakers interfere destructively at P, which is a quiet position ✓

parts.label: d
parts.question: Explain why the sound at a quiet position is very faint even though both loudspeakers are emitting sound.
markscheme: the two waves arrive half a cycle out of phase / with a phase difference of $\pi$ (a compression from one loudspeaker arrives together with a rarefaction from the other) ✓

by the principle of superposition the displacements add to give a resultant of (almost) zero amplitude, so very little sound energy reaches the ear (not exactly zero, because the two waves have travelled different distances and so have slightly different amplitudes) ✓

parts.label: e
parts.question: The frequency of the signal generator is doubled. Predict, with a reason, what happens to the separation of neighbouring quiet positions along the line.
markscheme: the wavelength halves (to 0.400 m), because the speed of sound is unchanged ✓
neighbouring quiet positions differ in path difference by one wavelength, so they move closer together / their separation is roughly halved ✓

v.what: speed of sound in the hall

d1.what: distance from loudspeaker 1 to the point P

d2.what: distance from loudspeaker 2 to the point P

parts.label: a
parts.examinerNote: Coherence is a constant phase difference (which requires the same frequency). "They are in phase" alone is accepted as a special case of a constant phase difference.

parts.label: c
parts.examinerNote: Path difference 2.00 m = 2.5 wavelengths, so destructive interference. The conclusion must follow from the comparison with the wavelength; "quiet" without the path difference earns nothing.

parts.label: d
parts.examinerNote: Two points: antiphase arrival, then superposition giving a minimum amplitude. The bracketed remark on unequal amplitudes is not required for the mark.

parts.label: e
parts.examinerNote: λ = v/f halves. Successive minima are one wavelength apart in path difference, so the pattern becomes finer. Students may argue by analogy with the fringe spacing; the path-difference reason is what is asked for.
